item.title: After 49 Years, Voyager 1 Is a Mind-Blowing One Light-Day From Earth
item.description: Launched in 1977, the hardy spacecraft is still sending messages back home from a staggering distance in interstellar space.
item.dc:creator: Nadia Drake

item.title: How Much Do You Know About NASA’s Voyager Mission?
item.description: Voyagers 1 and 2 have gone farther and lasted longer than any other spacecraft that humans have sent out into the cosmos. Test your knowledge about their epic and ongoing journey.
item.dc:creator: The New York Times

item.title: Inca Children Were Given Cocaine and Ayahuasca Before Being Sacrificed
item.description: A toxicological study of frozen mummies from the Andes sheds light on what happened before a sacred ritual of the Inca Empire.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway

item.title: How Virtual Cells Could Transform Medicine
item.description: Biotechs are racing to create A.I. models of human cells, hoping to speed drug development and slow aging. Can computers match the complexity of life?
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer

item.title: What Can Genes Reveal About Chronic Pain?
item.description: The largest genetic study of pain to date identified new biological roots in the brain — and gave hints for research into both prevention and treatment.
item.dc:creator: Emily Baumgaertner Nunn
item.media:description: Blood samples at a biobank. The study pooled genetic and health records from more than 1.2 million people across three large biobanks with the aim of mapping chronic pain’s genetic architecture.

item.title: Fearing Chinese Rivals, U.S. Biotech Adopts a New Norm: Share Nothing
item.description: Concerns that well-funded Chinese companies will swoop in to grab new ideas for their own drug development are shaping an industry unaccustomed to such secrecy.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:description: Fears that Chinese companies will seize on biotech discoveries in the U.S. and quickly beat them to market with their own inventions or slightly altered dupes have prompted American companies to keep their discoveries secret.

item.title: How the Measles Virus Makes Your Immune System Forget
item.description: The United States has lost its measles-elimination status, signaling the return of a virus that can cause lasting health consequences.
item.dc:creator: David Quammen

item.title: A New, Bold Antarctic Rescue: Bringing Shackleton’s Outpost Back to Life
item.description: An abandoned station manager’s villa — the site of a historic effort to save the explorer’s marooned crew — has now been restored. Take a tour inside.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.category: South Georgia Museum (Grytviken, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands)

item.title: Scientists Are Stumped by This Strange Object in Space
item.description: The rocky body called 1998 KY26 is moving in ways that gravity alone cannot explain. So far, no one knows why.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Nazaryan

item.title: White House Withdraws Nomination of Heidi Overton to Be F.D.A. Commissioner
item.description: The Senate health committee was scheduled to vote on her nomination Wednesday morning after wrestling with concerns about her stance on abortion and vaccines.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett
item.media:description: Dr. Heidi Overton during a Senate committee hearing in September.

item.title: Judge Finds Trump’s Planned Seabed Mining Auction Violated Law
item.description: It’s unclear whether the Trump administration will proceed with a lease sale set for Thursday to permit companies to mine the ocean floor off American Samoa.
item.dc:creator: Quinn Glabicki
item.media:description: A portion of the deep-sea floor observed during the 2026 NOAA American Samoa expedition in August.

item.title: A.I.’s People-Pleasing Problem
item.description: A new report found that popular chatbots often abandon scientific facts to affirm users’ beliefs.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Moens
item.media:credit: Andria Lo for The New York Times
item.media:description: Researchers tested 33 of the most widely used A.I. chatbots on tasks aimed at revealing potential climate disinformation risks.

item.title: There’s a New Push at COP31 in Turkey: Electrification
item.description: With war squeezing global oil and gas supplies, leaders at COP31 are backing a plan that would mirror China’s rapid grid expansion.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan
item.category: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
item.media:description: A solar farm in Qinghai Province, China, last year. The country makes 80 percent of the world’s solar panels.

item.title: A More Precise Clock Is on Its Way
item.description: The optical atomic clock, which scientists say would be off by about a second over 14 billion years, is soon expected to become a primary reference.
item.dc:creator: Penelope Colston
item.category: International Bureau of Weights and Measures
National Institute of Standards and Technology
item.media:credit: Juho Kuva for The New York Times
item.media:description: To measure time, optical clocks use a laser to probe atoms that have been isolated and cooled to a near standstill. The photo shows compact lasers made by the Finnish company Vexlum, which is working with Menlo Systems on commercial production of an optical clock.

item.title: Pipeline Executive Worked for Alan Armstrong During Permitting Push
item.description: Senator Alan Armstrong hired his former company’s top lawyer temporarily, while the chamber drafted a sweeping energy bill. Ethics officials signed off on the unusual arrangement.
item.dc:creator: Evan Halper
item.media:description: Senator Alan Armstrong, Republican of Oklahoma, speaking to reporters at the Capitol in September.

item.title: John H. Powers III to Lead NIAID Amid Turmoil
item.description: Dr. John H. Powers III was appointed director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, a powerful post held for decades by Dr. Anthony Fauci.

item.category: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
item.media:credit: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases

item.title: Permitting Bill Would Charge Data Centers Billions for Power
item.description: The permitting bill could make it easier to build data centers for A.I. but a novel provision would also force data centers to pay much more for power.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:description: A data center under construction in Abilene, Texas, which is one of the largest data center hubs.

item.title: How to Watch the 2026 Leonids Meteor Shower
item.description: Known for bright, fast meteors with long tails, the Leonids come around every November. But the number of streaks visible per hour can be low.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller
item.media:description: The Leonid meteor shower over North Macedonia in 2020.

item.title: This Cancer Kills Children in a Year. Research Has Been Stalled for a Year.
item.description: For 27 years, the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium worked to save kids with brain cancer. But just before 5-year-old Ryleigh Schecter was diagnosed, the government shut it down.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Miller and Lexi Parra

item.title: F.D.A. Rejects Closely Watched Lung Cancer Drug From China
item.description: The treatment, called ivonescimab, has become a symbol of China’s rise in drug development.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Robbins
item.media:credit: James Cavallini/Universal Images Group, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Summit Therapeutics of Florida had been seeking to bring to the U.S. market a drug for lung cancer, called ivonescimab, that was invented in China.

item.title: ‘Birdbrain’ Is a Misnomer. Crows Make Decisions Faster Than We Can
item.description: In a recent experiment, crows could process and respond to visual cues at twice the speed as humans and monkeys.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mitchell Brown

item.title: SpaceX Makes History With Successful Rocket Catch in Texas
item.description: The Starship spacecraft returned from orbit to the same spot where it lifted off, marking a key milestone in SpaceX’s vision of building fully reusable rockets.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:description: SpaceX’s Starship successfully returned from orbit and was captured on the launchpad on Saturday afternoon in Starbase, Texas.

item.title: SpaceX is betting mechanical arms can ‘catch’ its reusable rockets.
item.dc:creator: Mack Liederman
item.media:description: Starship launched on Friday from SpaceX’s “Mechazilla” tower. The company is planning for the tower’s mechanical arms to catch the returning rocket on Saturday.

item.title: Starship will play a big role in Artemis III.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:description: An Orion spacecraft sitting on top of the Space Launch System rocket before the Artemis II mission. During Artemis III, Orion will try to dock with Starship.

item.title: Inside Starfactory, where Starships are born.

item.media:description: SpaceX gave reporters a tour of the Starship manufacturing facility in Texas on Friday, but did not allow any photographs or videos to be taken inside.

item.title: These Killer Female Apes Challenge the ‘Man the Hunter’ Origin Story
item.description: Bonobos are as closely related to humans as chimps. New evidence that female bonobos are the primary hunters could radically alter our understanding of early human societies.
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mitchell Brown

item.title: Malawi Lacks Money to Fund its El Niño Plans
item.description: The question is being asked across the developing world, where hunger risk is high from the extreme weather El Niño is expected to bring. Malawi has a big plan, but little money.
item.dc:creator: Chico Harlan, Golden Matonga and Joao Silva
item.media:description: Tilling a field in anticipation of the seasonal rains in Namasoko, a village in the Phalombe district in southern Malawi.

item.title: The Russian Scientist Behind the Deadly Novichok Nerve Agents Has Died
item.description: Vladimir Uglev, a lead developer of a Cold War-era chemical weapon used on the dissident Alexei Navalny, later turned against the government. He was 80.
